findings.title: Google refresh writes the Zod result wrapper into credential.key
findings.body: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the Zod SafeParse object ({ success, data }), not the parsed credential. GoogleCalendarService assigns that return value straight to key and prisma.credential.update persists it. This runs on every access-token refresh even when credential sync is disabled (the old code stored googleCredentialSchema.parse(...), which returned the credential itself). After the first refresh the row is no longer a Google credential, so the next GoogleCalendarService constructor throws in googleCredentialSchema.parse and Google Calendar stops working until the user reconnects.

findings.title: Salesforce refresh calls prisma without an import and then uses the old access token
findings.body: getClient now always refreshes the Salesforce token and calls prisma.credential.update, but this file never imports prisma. Constructing SalesforceCalendarService therefore throws ReferenceError before any Event/Contact call, so the Salesforce integration is broken for every user, not only credential-sync deployments. The new token is also not what the client uses: jsforce.Connection is still created with credentialKey.access_token (the pre-refresh value) at line 106, and a new refresh_token from Salesforce is discarded in favor of the old one. Every calendar operation also pays an extra token round-trip, and this path never calls refreshOAuthTokens, so CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is ignored for Salesforce.

findings.title: Absent refresh_token is overwritten with the literal string "refresh_token"
findings.body: After a successful parse, if refresh_token is missing or empty the helper sets it to the string "refresh_token". Office365CalendarService then spreads tokenResponse.data onto the saved credential. Microsoft's refresh response often omits refresh_token (the Office 365 schema marks it optional, and the previous safeParse path left the stored token untouched). The real refresh token is replaced, the next refresh sends refresh_token=refresh_token, and Microsoft returns invalid_grant, permanently disconnecting Outlook calendar. This runs whether or not credential sync is enabled.

findings.title: Sync-mode token schema cannot match any real token payload
findings.body: minimumTokenResponseSchema is a z.object whose extra keys are the literal strings produced by z.string().toString() and z.string().optional().toString() (Zod type names / "[object Object]"), not wildcards, and the object is not passthrough. When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, every refresh goes through this schema. Real bodies only have access_token and an expiry field, so safeParse always fails and the helper throws "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Google, Office 365, Zoom, and Salesforce token refresh cannot succeed in sync mode, and the comment's intent (treat any numeric field as expiry and keep other properties) is not implemented.

findings.title: Sync refresh returns a raw Fetch Response that callers do not understand
findings.body: When credential sync is on, refreshOAuthTokens returns the Fetch Response and never checks response.ok or reads response.json(). Callers were not updated to that contract: Google reads res.data (gaxios), HubSpot treats the result as a HubspotToken (accessToken/expiresIn), Zoho Bigin and Zoho CRM read axios .data and persist it, and Lark passes the body to handleLarkError which expects Lark's { code, data } envelope. A sync response of { access_token, expiry } therefore throws or is written into credential.key as the wrong shape. Non-2xx responses are also treated as success. Turning on the new env vars breaks token refresh for those apps instead of delegating it.

findings.title: Outbound token sync request carries no authentication
findings.body: The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only calcomUserId and appSlug as form fields. It does not send CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET, a signature, or any other credential, and it does not require HTTPS. .env.example presents this as configuration-only, and the helper comment says the response should contain the access token. Anyone who can reach that URL can request third-party access tokens for any Cal user id. Those tokens are then stored and used as the user's Google/Zoom/Microsoft credentials. The inbound webhook authenticates with a shared secret, but the outbound call that actually returns live tokens does not.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin passes credential id where the sync API expects user id
findings.body: refreshOAuthTokens' third argument is the Cal.com user id (sent as calcomUserId). BiginCalendarService.refreshAccessToken passes credentialId instead. With sync enabled, the parent app looks up the wrong user and can return that user's access token; the following code persists tokenInfo.data onto this credential. Even before response parsing is fixed, the parent is asked to mint or rotate tokens for an unrelated id. Other adapters pass credential.userId.

findings.title: Lark deletes the credential if the local refresh token is expired, before sync
findings.body: refreshAccessToken still deletes the credential and throws when refresh_token is missing or refresh_expires_date is past, and only then calls refreshOAuthTokens. Credential sync is supposed to obtain a new access token from CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT without a provider refresh token (that helper's comment says the response only contains an access token and expiry). For a synced Lark user whose stored refresh token is a placeholder or has expired, the row is deleted and the sync endpoint is never called, so the integration and its tokens are lost instead of refreshed.

findings.title: Zoom sync sends app slug "zoomvideo" instead of "zoom"
findings.body: refreshOAuthTokens is called with appSlug "zoomvideo", but the Zoom credential is stored with appId "zoom" (see the OAuth callback) and the app-store slug used by the new webhook is "zoom". The parent app, which keys credentials by the slug it posted to /api/webhook/app-credential, will not find a "zoomvideo" credential. Zoom token refresh via the sync endpoint fails or refreshes the wrong app, while every other adapter in this PR passes its real app slug (google-calendar, msteams, office365-calendar, and so on).

findings.title: Webhook find-then-create can insert duplicate app credentials
findings.body: The handler loads an existing credential with findFirst on (userId, appId) and, if none is found, creates one. There is no unique constraint on that pair (other OAuth callbacks in this PR delete duplicates because findFirst otherwise ignores them) and no transaction or retry on unique conflict. Two concurrent sync deliveries for the same user and app both observe no row and both insert. Later refreshes and calendar lookups also use findFirst without a stable order, so they can keep using a stale duplicate while the webhook updates a different row.

findings.title: Sync update leaves invalid credentials marked invalid
findings.body: When a credential already exists, the webhook updates only key. It does not set invalid: false. Adapters in this PR (Google, Webex, Zoom) set invalid: true after an unrecoverable refresh, and credential loading skips invalid rows. A later successful sync from the parent app therefore stores new tokens on a row that is still treated as disconnected, so calendar and video calls keep failing until the user deletes and reinstalls the app.

findings.title: No tests cover token persistence or the credential webhook
findings.body: The PR adds the credential webhook, parseRefreshTokenResponse, and refreshOAuthTokens, and the author notes that no tests were added. There is no unit test that the object written to credential.key is still the provider credential (Google currently persists the SafeParse wrapper) or that a refresh response without refresh_token keeps the previous refresh token (Office 365 now stores the literal "refresh_token"). Those regressions ship on the normal, sync-disabled refresh path and would be caught by a test that asserts the saved key.
